title: Rogue Waves
objective: After this level you can explain giant rogue waves.
summary: A rogue wave is more than twice the size of the waves around it. The Draupner wave, 25.6 m high on January 1, 1995, proved sailors' stories true.

cards.headline: For centuries, sailors described walls of water. Scientists doubted them.
cards.body: Then, on New Year's Day 1995, a laser on a gas platform in the North Sea measured one. The sailors had been right all along.

cards.headline: Big for the neighborhood
cards.body: A rogue wave isn't simply a big wave in a big storm. NOAA defines it by comparison: more than twice the size of the waves around it. Rogues are very unpredictable, often charge in from a different direction than the wind and the other waves, and tend to look like walls of water, steep-sided with unusually deep troughs. It's not just the size of the wave. It's the size of the surprise.

mascot.line: Rogue means big for the neighborhood, not just big. The comparison is what counts.

cards.fact: The Draupner wave stood 25.6 m high.
cards.context: Around the platform that day, the significant wave height (roughly the average of the highest third of waves) was almost 12 m. Draupner was more than twice that: a rogue by definition, caught by an instrument instead of a shaken sailor. The measurement confirmed that giant rogue waves are real.

cards.headline: When waves add up
cards.body: So where do rogues come from? Swells from different storms travel at different speeds and in different directions. Now and then their crests line up and reinforce each other, stacking into a towering wave that soon disappears. Rogues also form where storm waves run into a current flowing the other way, such as the Gulf Stream or the Agulhas Current, and those tend to last longer. Ordinary waves plus bad timing: one extraordinary wave.

cards.headline: Rogue waves: confirmed
learned: Rogue: more than twice the waves around it
Crests that line up can stack

questions.prompt: On New Year's Day 1995, a laser on the Draupner gas platform recorded _____.

options.label: a North Sea tsunami
options.rationale: It was a single giant storm wave, not a tsunami.

options.label: a 25.6 m wave in 12 m seas
an underwater landslide
options.rationale: The laser measured the sea surface.

questions.explanation: On January 1, 1995, the Draupner laser measured a 25.6 m wave when the significant wave height was almost 12 m.

questions.prompt: Match each part of the Draupner story with its detail.

pairs.left: A laser on a gas platform

questions.explanation: A laser on a gas platform measured the Draupner wave on New Year's Day 1995. It was 25.6 m high, more than twice the significant wave height of almost 12 m.

questions.prompt: Swell from distant storms can cross whole oceans. How can two sets of swell build a rogue wave?

options.label: Their crests line up and reinforce each other
They cancel out and leave a deep hole in the sea
options.rationale: Canceling makes the sea smaller, not a rogue.

options.label: They freeze together in cold water
options.rationale: Temperature has nothing to do with it.

options.label: They pull the tide up with them
options.rationale: Rogues come from waves adding up, not from tides.

questions.explanation: Swells traveling at different speeds and directions sometimes coincide, and their crests stack into a towering wave.
